title: The Price of a Nap
summary: A miserly landlord charges a weary traveler for sleeping in the shadow of his wall. Birbal settles the account with the movement of the sun.
full_text:
On a scorching summer afternoon in Agra, when the hot Loo winds blew across the plains, an exhausted peasant named Bhola was carrying a heavy sack of grain toward the city market. Drenched in sweat and dizzy from the blistering heat, Bhola stopped beside the high stone boundary wall of a wealthy merchant named Seth Lalchand.

Finding a cool patch of dark shadow cast by the merchant's wall onto the public dusty road, Bhola rested his head on his sack and fell into a peaceful twenty-minute nap.

Presently, Seth Lalchand walked out of his iron gate. Seeing the peasant sleeping in the shadow of his wall, the miser poked Bhola with his walking stick: 'Wake up, you freeloader! Pay me five copper coins!'

Bhola rubbed his eyes: 'For what, master? I am lying on the public street!'

Lalchand shouted: 'You slept in the shadow of my wall! My wall cost two thousand rupees to build! The shadow belongs to my wall, and therefore belongs to me! If you enjoy my private shadow, you must pay for it!'

The ridiculous quarrel reached the ears of Emperor Akbar, who was sitting in the Diwan-i-Am. Akbar looked at Birbal with amusement: 'Can a man own a shadow?'

Birbal said: 'Seth Lalchand's claim must be settled with scientific justice.'

Birbal said to the merchant: 'Sethji, you are entirely right. You built the wall, so you own the shadow cast by the wall.'

Lalchand beamed: 'Thank you, wise minister!'

'However,' Birbal continued, pointing out the arched window at the afternoon sun, 'as the sun moves across the sky, your wall's shadow stretches out and covers twenty feet of the Emperor's public roadway!

'The public roadway belongs to the crown. Therefore, for every hour your private shadow encroaches upon the Emperor's road, you are trespassing and obstructing imperial traffic!

'You must pay the royal treasury a rental fee of twenty gold mohurs per hour for the land your shadow occupies! And since your shadow has fallen upon the road every afternoon for the last ten years, you owe the Emperor forty thousand gold coins!'

Lalchand turned pale as a corpse. His knees shook; he fell face-down on the floor, weeping: 'Mercy, Lord Birbal! I withdraw my claim! The shadow is free! The public may sleep in it forever!'

Akbar roared with laughter, fined the miser twenty silver coins to give to the poor peasant, and praised Birbal's brilliant legal turning of the tables.
moral: நீதி மற்றும் வாழ்க்கை பாடம்: Wit beats power
